segments.voice: Yesterday: Kusha and Lava, named for a handful of grass, singing their father's story before him without knowing it. Today, the last time Sita stands before Rama.

Sita's name means furrow. Back in the first book, King Janaka was plowing a field for a ritual when the plow turned up a baby girl in the earth. He raised her as his daughter and named her for the furrow she was found in. Hold on to that, because the Ramayana remembers it. Today the girl from the furrow, now the mother of two grown boys, is brought before a great assembly and asked, one more time, to prove herself.
screen: `SITA MEANS FURROW.` → `FOUND IN A PLOWED FIELD.` → `ASKED ONCE MORE TO PROVE HERSELF.`

segments.voice: When Rama learns the singing boys are his sons, he sends word to Valmiki: if Sita is pure, let her come and swear it here, before everyone, so the people can see. The next morning the assembly fills: sages, kings, ordinary people from every corner. Valmiki walks in first, and Sita follows, head bowed, hands folded. Valmiki speaks for her. These are your sons, he tells Rama, and Sita is blameless; he stakes on it all the merit of his long life of austerity. Rama answers that he believes it, and that he sent her away because of what people were saying. But the oath is still asked of her. Then Sita speaks. She makes three solemn declarations, each built the same way. If I have never thought of anyone but Rama, let the earth goddess open and give me a place. If I have honored him in mind, word and deed, let the earth receive me. As she finishes, the ground splits. A shining throne rises from below, held up by serpents, and the earth goddess herself takes Sita in her arms and seats her there. The throne sinks back down, and the earth closes. The assembly cries out. Rama is wild with grief, and angry at the earth itself. The girl found in a furrow has gone home to the ground she came from. And the poem doesn't say what to feel about it.
screen: `LET HER SWEAR IT BEFORE EVERYONE.` · `VALMIKI SPEAKS FOR HER.` · `IF I HAVE NEVER THOUGHT OF ANOTHER.` · `THE EARTH OPENS AND TAKES HER HOME.` · then, large: `THE GIRL FROM THE FURROW GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: If you can, put your bare feet flat on the ground, or sit on the floor, and feel your weight handed down into the earth. You don't have to hold yourself up right now; the ground is doing it, and with each out-breath you can let a little more weight go down.
Sita. Her name means furrow, the field where she was found, and the earth she returns to after her oath before the assembly.

howItsDone: Sita's return to the earth is told in Hindu homes, songs and stage plays, often with deep grief for her; devotees honor Sita as a goddess in her own right, linked with the earth and with Lakshmi.

original.note: Sanskrit sītā: the furrow a plow makes. Sita was found in one, and goes back into the earth.

chat.says: Why does Sita's story end with the earth taking her back?
options: She was found in a furrow, and after her oath the earth she came from received her.
The gods hid her below the earth to keep her safe from Ravana's allies.
Valmiki asked the earth to hide her until Rama came to apologize.
chat.meaning: Sita means furrow; she was found in the earth. After her oath before the assembly, the earth goddess took her home.
